title: Caring for kesh
hook: washing, combing and covering the hair as daily care

segments.voice: Yesterday, why a written code: it travels, it settles things fairly, it welcomes the newcomer. Your line was one code, many homes. Who did you show the ropes to? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

Early morning in a Sikh home. Someone sits on the edge of a bed with long hair down past the shoulders, still damp. A small wooden comb works through it from the ends up, slowly, patiently, one knot at a time. Then the hair is twisted, wound into a knot on top of the head, and covered. Outside that room, people mostly notice only the last step, the turban or the head covering. They rarely see the quiet minutes before it. We met kesh, uncut hair, earlier on this path, as one of the five Ks. Today isn't about the rule. It's about the morning.
screen: `DAMP HAIR, A WOODEN COMB.` → `TWISTED, KNOTTED, COVERED.` → `NOT THE RULE: THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code asks Sikhs to keep the hair uncut, and Sikhs speak of it as a gift kept as it was given. But keeping is a verb. It happens every day, and it has three parts. Washing comes first. Long hair has to be washed and dried with care, and it often becomes part of the early-morning bath before prayer, so the body is clean when the mind turns to the Name. Combing comes second. The kangha, the small comb, is itself one of the five Ks, kept in the hair. The code asks Sikhs to comb the hair, and the kangha is there so it can be done any time of day. Some Sikhs say a prayer or recite while they comb, so that tending the hair and remembering God happen together. Covering comes third. The hair is gathered up and covered, with a turban, a keski, a chunni or another covering, so it is kept clean and kept in honor. Notice what this does to a rule. Don't cut your hair is something you could keep by doing nothing at all. Caring for kesh asks for something every single morning. It turns a boundary into a small daily act of attention. It also turns the body into part of the practice. A Sikh doesn't only keep the hair; the hair keeps reminding the Sikh. Each tangle asks for patience. Each covering is a small act of respect. And tomorrow the comb comes out again. Daily care.
screen: `KEEPING IS A VERB.` · `WASHED BEFORE PRAYER.` · `COMBED WITH THE KANGHA.` · `COVERED, KEPT IN HONOR.` · then, large: `DAILY CARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comb your hair slowly. If you have a comb or brush nearby, pick it up. If your hair is short or gone, run your fingers over your head instead. Settle, and breathe. Start at the ends and work up, slowly, one stroke at a time. When you meet a knot, don't pull. Pause, and work it loose. Notice the feel of it, and your own hands caring for you. If you pray, you can remember God with each stroke. If not, just give the comb your full attention until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Caring for kesh. Washing, combing and covering the uncut hair, as a daily act of care and remembrance. Today's word.
Your line: daily care. Today, pick one thing you own or keep, a plant, a tool, your own body, and give it a few minutes of slow, deliberate care. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep kesh wash, comb and cover their hair as part of the daily routine, often in the early morning before prayer, using the kangha kept in the hair.

fork.setup: you've kept your hair uncut for years. is that the whole of kesh?
options: yes, not cutting is all it asks.
no: it's washing, combing and covering, every day.
fork.reveal: keeping is a verb. kesh asks for daily care, which turns a rule you could keep by doing nothing into a small daily act of attention.

notes: 'The code asks Sikhs to comb the hair' is stated without a number; the Sikh Rehat Maryada's wording on combing (some renderings say twice a day) should be confirmed before any number is added.
The early-morning bath before prayer is described as common ('often'); the code's guidance on rising early and bathing supports the habit, but please confirm or soften.
'Sikhs speak of it as a gift kept as it was given' is a general description; confirm.
Head coverings listed: turban, keski, chunni; confirm the list and that it is appropriate for all genders as phrased.
Editor pass: the code asks all Sikhs, not only the initiated, to keep the hair uncut, so the line was corrected; trimmed stock uplift ('nobody does it perfectly') and a stock phrase in the practice.
